sentences.text: In the present case petitioner in her evidence as PW1, specifically testified that while she was returning home from her college on her scooty, a Maruti Car no.DL-5CJ-8719 came at a very high speed being driven by respondent no.1 in a rash and negligent manner, hit the scooty of PW1 and thereafter dragged her for some distance.
PW1 further says that passersby made a call to the police at 100 number and caught the driver at some distance and brought back to the place of accident.
This aspect of the evidence of PW1 is well proved as nothing came in the cross examination of PW1 to disbelieve such version.
Rather PW1 was never cross examined on behalf of respondent no.1 (driver) and respondent no.2 (owner).

Moreover the evidence of PW1 gets corroboration from the contents of DAR including site plan, mechanical inspection report of the scooty of PW1 as well as the offending vehicle no.DL-5CJ-8719 and statement of MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.10 16:17:25 +0530 witnesses.
Thus this aspect is well proved on the record that accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of respondent o.1 while driving car no.DL-5CJ-8719.
Accordingly issue stands decided in favour of petitioner and against the respondents.
Issue No.2 11.
The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.

So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit;

3 (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, discomfort,
disappointment, hardship, frustration and mental stress in life."
12.

Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.10 16:17:33 +0530 computation of compensation in injury cases.

The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
4.

The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.10 16:17:48 +0530 consequence of the injuries.

Dar-Sakshi vs Himanshu on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88959949/
4 (v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage)
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii), (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
13.

In the light of the aforementioned judgments, the compensation to which the petitioner is entitled shall be as under:-
PECUNIARY DAMAGES :
Medical Expenses:
14.

PW1 in her deposition stated that after the accident she was taken to GTB Hospital where she remained confined to bed for 15 days on account of grievous injuries sustained by her on her left foot/leg and arms.
PW1 simply states that her parents spent Rs.60,000/- for medical expenses and private physiotherapy treatment, conveyance charges, special diet etc.
PW1 however in her evidence has not proved any documentary evidence to establish having spent Rs.60,000/- on the above said heads.

In such circumstances when there is otherwise no documentary evidence, however taking into consideration the MLC of the injured showing the nature of injuries to be simple, a sum of Rs.10,000/- is awarded under the head of medical expenses.
SHAILENDER MACT No.670/2017 MALIK  Date: 2024.05.10  16:17:56 +0530  Loss of studies:
15. As per the evidence of PW1 petitioner was a student of B.A. Hons. in History at the time of accident.
As such she was not earning any money.
However on account of the accidental injuries petitioner apparently remained confined to bed for about 15 days and kept on taking treatment for about one month.
Therefore keeping in view the education of the petitioner, petitioner is awarded sum of Rs.17,604/- being an amount equivalent to minimum wages of graduate worker at Delhi at the time of accident.

Special Diet & Conveyance Charges:

5 16.
No evidence has been led by petitioner to prove the fact that any special diet was prescribed or incurring of any conveyance charges.
However as per the MLC of the petitioner/injured and the evidence of PW1 she remained confined to bed for 15 days.
This Tribunal while assessing loss of studies of petitioner, awarded the compensation for an amount for one month loss of her studies.
Therefore in view of evidence of PW1 and MLC of petitioner/injured this Tribunal awards a sum of Rs.15,000/- each under the head of special diet and conveyance charges.

Attendant Charges:
17.
Though there is no evidence on the record with regard to expenditure made by the petitioner towards engaging any attendant for her proper upkeep during the period of her medical treatment.
However fact remains that due to accidental injuries petitioner remained confined to bed for 15 days which this Tribunal assessed to be one month period for loss of her studies.
In view of this position of the matter this Tribunal is of the view that petitioner is certainly entitled for attendant charges for the period she confined to bed.

Thus this Tribunal awards compensation of MACT No.670/2017 SHAILENDER MALIK Date: 2024.05.10 16:18:06 +0530 Rs.10,000/- to the petitioner under the above said head. NON PECUNIARY DAMAGES :
Pain & Sufferings:
18.

While discussing the criteria to ascertain the compensation for pain and sufferings by victim of vehicular accident, observations of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Satya Narain v. Jai Kishan, FAO No:
709/02, date of decision: 02.02.2007 can be considered:
"12. On account of pain and suffering, suffice would it be to note that it is difficult to measure pain and suffering in terms of a money value.
However, compensation which has to be paid must bear some objectives co-relation with the pain and suffering.

13. The objective facts relatable to pain and suffering would be:
(a) Nature of injury.
(b) Body part affected (c) Duration of the treatment."
19.
In this case, as per MLC of petitioner, she was found to have suffered injuries on her left foot, left forearm etc. which were opined by the doctor to be simple in nature.
It is the case of the petitioner that she continued her treatment even thereafter also.

Thus, in the considered view of this Tribunal an amount of Rs.25,000/- would be just and fair compensation for pain, sufferings and mental trauma suffered by the petitioner as consequences of injuries sustained in the accident.

Accordingly,
Rs.25,000/- is granted to the petitioner under this head.
Loss of Amenities:

6 20.

In view of the discussion made above regarding facts and circumstances of the present case,
evidence of petitioner/PW1 and injuries sustained by her in the accident in question, it would be appropriate to grant compensation to petitioner for loss of amenities.
Thus petitioner is SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.05.10 16:18:14 +0530 granted a compensation of Rs.10,000/- under this head.

21. Thus, the compensation awarded to the petitioner is summarized as under:-

Petitioner shall also be entitled to interest @ 8% per annum on the award amount from the date of filing of the petition till realization.
LIABILITY 24.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondent is liable to pay the compensation amount.

Question of liability arises in this case because insurance/respondent no.3 in its pleadings has pleaded that driving licence of respondent no.1 has not been verified by the concerned transport authority and found to be fake as per the report of ARTO Farrukhabad, Fatehgarh, UP.

To substantiate this aspect insurance company has examined two witness, PW R3W1 is Rajender Kumar, Assistant from ARTO Office Farrukhabad who brought the summoned record pertaining to DL No.4476/FBD/09 and stated that such licence is fake and never issued in the name of Himanshu s/o Shayam Singh (respondent no.1 herein).
Said MALIK

R3W2 is Raj Kumar, Assistant from respondent no.3/insurance company and stated that insurance policy no.35101031166138832115 was issued in the name of respondent no.2 Sandhya Mishra for vehicle no.DL- 5CJ-8719.

Witness states that a notice under Order 12 Rule 8 CPC was served to respondent no.1 and 2 which is Ex.R3W2/2.
26. Having considered the evidence when as per the evidence of R3W1 the licence of respondent no.1 as provided to IO of the case was found to be fake, same was also not got verified by the IO.
Moreover IO has also charge sheeted respondent no.1 beside offences u/s 279/337 IPC, for offence under section 471 IPC for having used a forged document.
Evidence of R3W1 was not cross examined at all on behalf of respondent no.1 and 2.

It can safely be concluded that respondent Dar-Sakshi vs Himanshu on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88959949/
